title: How do I know if it's a rough patch or the end?
summary: Rough patch or the end of the relationship? How bad it feels won't tell you. Three questions that will, and a simple way to test it.
body_markdown:
Short answer: you can't tell by how bad it feels. A rough patch can be miserable, with a fight every week and nights on the couch. The end of a relationship is often calm. So if you're trying to work out which one you're in, the amount of pain is the wrong thing to measure.


Three things tell you more. Whether the trouble has a starting point you can name. Whether both of you still want it to get better. And whether anything changes when one of you actually tries. The rest of this page is how to check each one.


## Why the loud version is often the better sign


People tend to assume that fighting a lot means it's ending. Often it's the reverse. If you're still arguing, you both still want something from each other. You're annoyed that they didn't ask about your day because you still want them to ask. Even[having the same argument over and over](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/we-keep-having-the-same-argument) means two people who haven't given up on getting through to each other.


The version to worry about more is the quiet one. You stop bringing things up, and not because they got solved. You just don't want to have the conversation anymore. They come home late and you notice you don't mind. That can look like peace. Usually it means one of you has stopped trying, and that is much closer to an ending than a bad fight is.


## Three questions that separate a rough patch from an ending


1. **Can you say when it started?** Rough patches usually have a beginning. A new baby, a layoff, a move, a parent getting sick, a year of money stress. You can remember what it was like before, and you want that back. When it's closer to the end, people struggle to find a "before." Or they find one and realize the same problem was there too, and they were just more willing to live with it.
2. **Do you both still want it fixed?** Not "are we both doing everything right." Just this: if you say "I hate how things are between us," does your partner agree and look worried, or shrug? And be honest about your own side. If they came to you tomorrow ready to change, would you be glad, or would you mostly feel tired?
3. **Does anything move when someone tries?** In a rough patch, effort gets a response. One good conversation and the next few days are easier. A small change gets noticed. Near the end, effort gets nothing back. You plan the dinner, it's fine, and by Tuesday it's as if it never happened.


One bad answer doesn't settle it. Everyone has months where the honest answer to all three is "not really." Three bad answers that have stayed the same for a long time tell you a lot.


## The argument you're still having in your head


There's a detail we notice in Maia conversations that people rarely think is important. When someone is in a rough patch, they talk about their partner constantly. What they said on Sunday. Why they'd say that. What they should have said back. They're replaying the fight in the shower and in the car, still trying to win it or fix it. They're angry, and the anger is pointed at one specific person.


People who are closer to the end sound different. Their partner hardly comes up. They talk about the lease, about what they'd tell their family, about how much lighter they felt the week their partner was away for work. The argument in their head has gone quiet. Things didn't get better. They've just stopped expecting an answer.


So here's a quick check. Are you still arguing with them in your head? If you are, some part of you is still in this.


## A rough patch doesn't stay a rough patch forever


This is the uncomfortable part. These aren't two fixed categories. A lot of endings started as rough patches that nobody dealt with. The stressful thing passed, but by then you'd both gotten used to not talking, and you ended up[more like roommates than partners](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/we-feel-like-roommates-not-partners) . Or you both agreed things had to change,[said you'd work on it, and then nothing changed](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/we-said-wed-work-on-it-and-nothing-changed) .


So "it's just a rough patch" is only good news if somebody does something about it. Waiting for it to pass on its own is the most common way a fixable problem stops being fixable.


## If you still can't tell, test it for a month


You don't have to figure this out by thinking harder. Pick the one thing that bothers you most and say it plainly, without the list of everything else. Something like:


> "I don't like how distant we've been since the summer, and I want us to fix it. Can we eat dinner together a few nights a week, phones away, and see if it helps?"


Then watch what happens over the next few weeks. You're not looking for a perfect result. You're looking for whether they try at all, whether they ever bring it up without being reminded, and whether you find yourself wanting it to work.


If they try, even clumsily, that's a rough patch with two people in it. If you've asked clearly more than once and you're still[the only one trying](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/im-the-only-one-trying-in-my-relationship) , then how you asked was never the problem. Whether they want to is. And if they try hard and you feel nothing, that tells you something about your own side.


Whatever you find, it beats guessing. If the real question turns out to be[whether to break up or keep trying](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/should-i-break-up-or-keep-trying) , you'll be answering it with something you actually saw, not just a bad feeling at 1am.


If you'd like help working out which one you're in, you can talk it through privately with Maia first and figure out what you'd actually want to say. And if you're both willing, Maia can lead a conversation with the two of you, so the one thing finally gets said out loud.
